name: Squintmaxxing

lead: Squintmaxxing means slightly narrowing the eyelids, in photos and in daily habit, to get the look called hunter eyes: a lower upper-lid line and a more intense, less wide-open gaze. It costs nothing and can be stopped at any time.

The chain is mechanical: narrowing the lids lowers the visible upper eyelid line and reduces the amount of eye shown, which proponents say changes the impression of the eye area. It is promoted on looksmax.org; no studies have tested whether it changes perceived attractiveness.

paras: People practise a small, relaxed narrowing in the mirror and in photos, aiming for a controlled look rather than a strained squint. The effect is visible immediately and is usually combined with other eye-area changes such as brows and posture.

Squinting is generally regarded as harmless; an ophthalmologist quoted on Wikipedia cites temporary headache from muscle tension as the only harm. Forum claims about wrinkles or temple balding have no published support.

angle.text: You narrow the eyelids slightly, in photos and in daily habit, to get the intense look called hunter eyes. It is a free, instant adjustment that lowers the upper-lid line. Its effect on how others rate your looks has not been studied.

lead: Squintmaxxing is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person habitually narrows the eyelids slightly, aiming for the look community members call "hunter eyes": a lower upper eyelid line, less visible white and a more intense, focused gaze. Proponents describe it as a free, instant adjustment that can make the eye area look more attractive in person and in photographs [1][2].

The idea overlaps with a technique used in portrait photography, the squinch, in which a subtle narrowing of the lower lid is used to replace a wide-eyed look with a confident one [3]. Squinting itself is a documented behaviour. Wikipedia notes that it is a reflex in bright light and can briefly sharpen vision in people with uncorrected refractive error, and an Oxford ophthalmologist quoted there says the belief that squinting damages eyesight is an old wives' tale, with temporary headache from prolonged muscle contraction the damage he cites [4]. No published studies have tested whether deliberate squinting changes perceived attractiveness.

paras: In looksmax.org usage the practice is a mild, held narrowing of the eyes, similar to the reflex in bright sun, that members try to keep up until it is automatic. Posters call people who do it constantly 'permasquinters' and say it suits some eye shapes and medial canthus types, adding the caution 'squint at your own risk' [1]. Others object that the proper term is 'squinching', borrowed from photography [3].

The muscle that closes the eyelids and narrows the aperture is the orbicularis oculi. Its orbital part is under conscious control and can furrow the brows to reduce glare, while its palpebral part acts involuntarily; its antagonist is the levator palpebrae superioris, which raises the upper lid [5]. A squint therefore lowers the upper lid and lifts the lower lid together, which is the change squintmaxxers are after.

'Hunter eyes' is community shorthand for a male eye area with a positive canthal tilt, little to no upper eyelid exposure and low-set eyebrows, likened to the eyes of a predatory animal. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article cites a June 2023 Vice report for the definition [6]. That report describes the look as narrow, deep-set and hooded, with the opposite 'prey eyes' described as a negative tilt perceived as weak, and says proponents claim it makes a man seem more dominant and mysterious [2].

The Vice piece reported that videos tagged 'hunter eyes' had about 49.6 million views on TikTok, naming celebrities such as Chris Hemsworth, David Gandy, Robert Pattinson and Timothée Chalamet as examples. It listed ways people pursue the look: canthoplasty and other cosmetic surgery, mewing, bonesmashing and squinting, which it described as a cheaper alternative [2]. Indiana cosmetic surgeon Barry Epley said many reference photos show models squinting, and London clinician Ross Perry said the look is hard to reach without surgery because anatomy must be corrected [2].

The term 'squintmaxxing' appears in looksmax.org threads, including a 'daily reminder' thread and a 2021 guide that jokes about celebrity 'professional permasquinters' [1][7]. The practice rose alongside the broader spread of looksmaxxing slang on TikTok and forums in the early 2020s, when hunter eyes became a common talking point [2][6].

Squinting as a presentation technique has an older, separate history. The headshot photographer Peter Hurley teaches the squinch and describes it as a subtle narrowing of the distance between the lower eyelid and the pupil; his blog post of August 2022 on a Good Morning America appearance links the squinch to a look that combines confidence with approachability while keeping the image authentic [3].

Wikipedia notes that squinting in film often signals mystery, suspicion, toughness or desire, citing Clint Eastwood as a performer associated with the expression, from stoicism in The Good, the Bad and the Ugly to romantic longing in The Bridges of Madison County [4]. The critic Manohla Dargis is quoted there joking that eyes may be windows to the soul but men like Eastwood prefer the shades partly drawn [4].

The eyes also take part in smiling. In a Duchenne smile the orbicularis oculi raises the cheeks and forms crow's feet, a pattern the Wikipedia article on the smile associates with positive emotion, and it contrasts this with a smile that involves only the mouth [8]. Photographers who teach the squinch describe a similar narrowing of the lower lid used to avoid a wide-eyed look [3].

Squinting reduces the light entering the eye and filters off-axis rays, which can briefly sharpen vision for people with uncorrected refractive error; it is also a reflex in bright light, especially for light-coloured eyes [4]. Healthy pupils take about five minutes to adjust to a change of light, and squinting with pain beyond that period can indicate photophobia, a symptom with causes that include eye disease and migraine [4][9].

Wikipedia's article on the orbicularis oculi notes that repeated contraction pulls the skin toward the inner corner of the eye and that, with ageing, such folds become permanent crow's feet [5]. No published study has examined whether habitual deliberate squinting changes eyelid shape, wrinkles or perceived attractiveness.

One looksmax.org thread asks whether squinting could contribute to hair loss at the temples, with users reporting anecdotes about temple balding and tense muscles around the eye, and a reply recommending injections into the muscle for tension headaches [10]. No published research supports a link between squinting and balding. Posters in guide threads also warn about overdoing it and say to proceed carefully [1].

Related eye-area interventions discussed alongside hunter eyes include canthoplasty, brow and tear trough procedures, mewing and bonesmashing; surgeons quoted by Vice describe the first group as costly and multi-step [2]. Portrait photographers use the squinch, and many people squint reflexively in sunlight [4][3].

lore.intro: Squintmaxxing is promoted on looksmax.org as a free, instant improvement; discussion is mostly guide threads and jokes rather than data, and sits within the broader hunter eyes conversation [1][7][2].
